blocks.text: A plate of pounded yam and egusi soup is far too complex for your cells to use. Starch molecules are thousands of units long and proteins are folded chains. Digestion is the nine-metre journey that takes food apart, molecule by molecule, until it is small enough to cross into your blood.

blocks.markdown:
## What digestion means

Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones that can be absorbed into the blood.

It happens in two ways at once. **Mechanical digestion** is physical: chewing by the teeth, churning by the stomach muscles, and emulsification of fat by bile. It increases the surface area for enzymes to work on but changes no chemical. **Chemical digestion** uses enzymes to break the bonds in each molecule.

Food is pushed along the whole canal by **peristalsis** — waves of contraction of the circular and longitudinal muscles in the gut wall. This is why an astronaut, or someone standing on their head, can still swallow.

### The journey, region by region

**Mouth** — teeth cut and grind the food. Saliva from three pairs of glands moistens it and supplies salivary amylase, which begins to break starch into maltose. Saliva is slightly alkaline. The tongue rolls the food into a bolus and swallowing pushes it into the oesophagus.

**Oesophagus** — a muscular tube; no digestion occurs, only peristalsis.

**Stomach** — gastric glands secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, pepsin and rennin. The acid gives a pH of about 2, which kills most swallowed bacteria and provides the acid conditions pepsin needs. Pepsin begins protein digestion, converting protein to peptides. Salivary amylase is destroyed by the acid, so starch digestion pauses here. Food leaves as a creamy fluid called chyme.

**Duodenum** — two secretions arrive. **Bile** from the liver, stored in the gall bladder, contains no enzymes; it neutralises the acid and emulsifies fat into tiny droplets. **Pancreatic juice** contains pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase.

**Ileum** — intestinal juice completes digestion with maltase, peptidase (erepsin) and lipase, and this is where almost all absorption happens.

**Colon (large intestine)** — no digestion; water and mineral salts are reabsorbed, and bacteria act on the residue.

**Rectum and anus** — faeces are stored and then egested.

blocks.title: Emulsification
blocks.text: The physical breaking of large fat globules into many tiny droplets by bile salts. It is not chemical digestion, because the fat is still fat — but the vastly increased surface area lets lipase work far faster.

blocks.markdown:
### The ileum: built for absorption

Absorption is the passage of digested food from the gut into the blood, and the ileum is superbly adapted for it. Picture the inner surface: it is thrown into large folds, each fold carries thousands of finger-like **villi** about one millimetre long, and every cell on a villus has its own microscopic projections, the **microvilli**. Together these give an absorbing surface of roughly 200 square metres — about the size of a tennis court packed inside your abdomen.

Each villus is one cell thick, so diffusion distance is minimal. Inside it runs a dense network of blood capillaries to carry away glucose and amino acids, and a single **lacteal** — a lymph vessel — to carry away the products of fat digestion. Blood flow keeps the concentration gradient steep, and glucose and amino acids are also taken up by active transport when their concentration in the gut is low. The ileum is also very long, so food is in contact with the surface for a long time.

blocks.title: Following a slice of bread through the gut
blocks.prompt: A student eats bread, which is mainly starch with some protein and a little fat. Trace what happens to the starch from mouth to blood.

steps.text: In the mouth, teeth grind the bread and salivary amylase in the alkaline saliva starts converting starch to maltose.
In the stomach the pH falls to about 2. Amylase is denatured by this acid, so starch digestion stops temporarily while protein digestion by pepsin begins.
In the duodenum, alkaline bile and pancreatic juice neutralise the acid. Pancreatic amylase resumes the conversion of the remaining starch into maltose.
In the ileum, maltase in the intestinal juice splits each maltose molecule into two molecules of glucose, which is the final product of starch digestion.
Glucose is absorbed through the wall of a villus by diffusion and active transport into the blood capillaries.

The blood carries the glucose in the hepatic portal vein to the liver, which stores the excess as glycogen; the rest travels to the cells, where it is used in respiration. This final use of absorbed food is assimilation.

blocks.answer: Starch → maltose (salivary amylase, mouth) → paused in the stomach → maltose (pancreatic amylase, duodenum) → glucose (maltase, ileum) → absorbed into the blood capillaries of a villus and carried to the liver.

blocks.title: Bile contains no enzymes
blocks.text: Bile is a common trap. It is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and it emulsifies fat and neutralises stomach acid. But it contains no enzyme at all, so it never appears in the enzyme column of a table.

blocks.title: Answer in the right units
blocks.text: If a question asks for the end product of protein digestion, write 'amino acids', not 'peptides' — peptides are intermediates. Likewise the end products of fat digestion are 'fatty acids and glycerol', and of carbohydrate digestion, 'glucose'.

points: Digestion breaks large insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones, mechanically and chemically.
Starch becomes glucose, protein becomes amino acids, and fat becomes fatty acids and glycerol.
The stomach is acidic for pepsin; the duodenum and ileum are alkaline for pancreatic and intestinal enzymes.
Bile emulsifies fat and neutralises acid but contains no enzymes.
The ileum is adapted for absorption by villi and microvilli, a one-cell-thick wall, a rich capillary network and a lacteal.
